title: Sisters' piano lessons, the graphophone and forbidden blues records
summary: He tagged along to his sisters' lessons, loved the family graphophone and hid Bessie Smith records his churchgoing parents wanted to get rid of.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Well, let's go back to the --
To Muskogee and the family. Well, we talked about your father and mother and your sisters, but
now when do you start to get -- you know, when does music start to enter your life?

Well, I'll tell you, I really -- I used to go to take my sisters, you know, go along with them when they would take their lesson. My mother gave them lessons. The family was poor and so she would try to give the girls lessons. Well, the two older girls, they didn't care anything about it at all and then the next girl, she took some interest in it, you know, no more than just your --
Read, you know, and she did better than the other two. The other two, they didn't care anything about it and didn't try to do anything and --
Did you have a piano in the house then?

We did have a piano in the house and the first thing that ever made me think about any music was the fact that we had a old graphophone -- we called them graphophone in those days -- with the old bulldog up there sitting up there and this horn went out, you know?

So sometimes my dad would bring records from the furniture store and he didn't know what he was bringing. So, you know what I mean. If he brought Blue Heaven, he thought that was great because he liked Blue Heaven, see? Or if he
brought some church songs, that was great, you know? But one day, he brought a Mamie Smith or a Bessie Smith record --
-- and he put it on and I liked it, you know, but he says, "We're going to get rid of that record."
Were your mother and father sort of church-going people?

They were church-going people. Both church-going. And they would frown upon those kind of records, you know, but I'd always make it my business to try to hide the records and before they could get rid of them, I'd hide them somewhere. I'd get rid of the records for them, you know, and so, you know, when I was in school -- you know when you're in school, there's always a music teacher that comes around, you know, and I had never given any thought to music one way or the other and there was a teacher named Elsie Clark -- well, I'm sure she was up in age, but she would come around and that's when they had you singing from -- you know, you just sing, they would teach you the songs orally, you know.
